headline: Show HN: Musset, open-source Scrivener alternative with an AI that never writes
content:
A Mac writing app for people who finish books.

musset.app · Download for Mac · Compared with Scrivener, Ulysses, iA Writer and Manuskript

Free while it is a beta, then US$9.90 once from version 1.0, and open source either way. macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon.

Musset is as calm as a blank page, as structured as a manuscript, and as fast on the keyboard as WordStar. It has an editor inside who reads, questions and annotates, and who never writes a word for you. Your book stays a folder of plain text files with its whole history, in English, French, German, Spanish, Italian or Portuguese, typeset in EB Garamond when it is time to print.

Writing tools tend to choose one of three things: a calm editor, a manuscript organiser, or a machine that writes for you. Musset is the first two, and refuses the third.

Choose the keys your hands already know in Settings › Keyboard. One mode at a time; ⌘ stays Musset’s in every mode, and AZERTY keyboards are handled.

The command bar (⌘K) does everything else: go to any chapter or scene in any of your books, run a critique, search the text, change the appearance, export.

No more chapter-3-final-v2-REAL.docx. Musset quietly keeps every state of your book as you write: you never save a copy, never rename a file, and nothing you delete is ever really gone.

Behind it is git, the system the software world relies on to keep track of its work. You never have to see it.

Corrections are stored as CriticMarkup in the chapter itself — plain text, readable anywhere: {++added++}, {--deleted--}, {~~old~>new~~}, {==highlighted==}{>>comment<<}, followed by {@Name} for who made it.

The AI reads like a good editor: it quotes your sentence, says what it sees, and asks a question. It never rewrites your book.

The AI runs through your own account with the provider, signed in from Musset: Claude through the official Claude Code command-line tool, ChatGPT through the official Codex command-line tool. Musset holds no AI provider keys and takes no margin.

Each book has its language and variant (Book Settings). Musset applies its typography as you type, and checks spelling and grammar with LanguageTool, which runs inside Musset, on your Mac: nothing is sent anywhere. Brazilian and European Portuguese each have their own interface.

Reading mode typesets the chapter or the whole book next to the text, as it will print.

PDFs are typeset like a book, with Typst and EB Garamond:

Manuscripts for submission follow each country’s conventions, and count the way publishers count:

Entering a literary prize? Send the manuscript under a pseudonym, without your name or contact. Musset also exports Word (.docx, with styles your editor can use) and EPUB.

The welcome screen opens a book that already exists, and leaves the original untouched:

Musset is free while it is a beta. From version 1.0 it will cost US$9.90, once. It stays open source under the GPL: you may always build it yourself from this repository.

Musset Sync (€4.99 a month) is the optional service behind it:

Sync is built on git: Musset pushes and pulls your book’s history; nothing about your files changes.

A book is a folder. Musset reads and writes only its chapter files, the bible/ folder and the hidden .musset/ folder; everything else in the folder is left alone.

Download the DMG from musset.app, open it and drag Musset to Applications. It is signed and notarized by Apple, and updates itself from then on.

Requires macOS 14 Sonoma or later on Apple silicon. A build for Intel Macs is being tested: see issue 1.

You need Xcode 26.5 (older versions may not compile it), Rust and XcodeGen.

The first build downloads and checks, each against a pinned SHA-256, into ~/Library/Caches/Musset-build:

Typst is not a separate program: it is built into Musset as a library, by scripts/build-typeset.sh.

A signed, notarized DMG (needs a Developer ID and notary credentials stored with xcrun notarytool store-credentials AC_NOTARY):

By default the app is built for Apple silicon. MUSSET_ARCHS="arm64 x86_64" builds one app for both chips, MUSSET_ARCHS=x86_64 one for Intel alone.

package.sh signs the bundled tools, the Java runtime and the native libraries inside LanguageTool’s jars, notarizes the app and the DMG, staples both, and checks the result with Gatekeeper.

To run the tests while using Musset, give them their own build folder and bundle id, so the open app is untouched:

Tests that read the author’s own books skip themselves here: those books are not in this repository.

Some tests run only on request, because they call an AI, need a real book or render screenshots. They are skipped unless their environment variable is set (prefixed with TEST_RUNNER_ when passed to xcodebuild):

Interface text is written in English in the code and looked up in Musset/Resources/Localization/<language>.json:

Issues and pull requests are welcome. A few principles guide what goes in:

Musset is free software, released under the GNU General Public License, version 3 — see LICENSE. The programs and fonts bundled with the app keep their own licences, listed in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md.

“Musset” and its icon identify the official app; please give a modified version another name.

headline: ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
content:
An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card.

Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age.

It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed.

I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects.

From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier.

Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware?

And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent?

I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box.

As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle.

Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off.

The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS.

Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API.

One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running.

The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand.

ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a WG.EXE under 10 KB.

Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor:

Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS opens the note it saved in C:\MEMORY, finds the latest build, and recalls the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA.

That Run call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made, 320x200 in four colours, 16 KB:

Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them Claude says what it is about to do.

Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC speaker in GW-BASIC’s PLAY language.

A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy.

Eighteen tools. Claude works on the machine through these:

A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM), Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from your own floppy images in external/. All of them are proven on the 8088, and ClawDOS knows how to drive each one.

Memories and skills. Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit the task. F4 browses the memories:

Safe mode. On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port asks Allow ...? (y/n) first. F3 turns it off.

Conversations that last. Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too.

Any model, mid-conversation. /model lists the providers in CLAWDOS.CFG and switches between them and their models without losing the conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that speaks the Messages API works.

Easy on a slow link. The system prompt and tools are cached by the API. After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is new, so a tool result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API is retried, and the turn carries on.

A flight recorder. CLAWDOS.LOG has a line for every round: time to first token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads.

docs/API.md has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back.

You need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On Windows the command is python.

No key? python3 tunnel/mockapi.py plays the API offline: type CLAWDOS 10.0.2.2:18023 and send !help.

On a real PC: build with the address of the machine running the tunnel (python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443), copy CLAWDOS.IMG to the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu, boot, and type CLAWDOS. Later builds update the card’s image in place and keep its memories and chats (python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG).

/model, /chats, /memories, /new and /quit work from the input box. CLAWDOS -m "..." sends a message from the command line and -c NAME reopens a chat.

ClawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version: see LICENSE. HARNESS.EXE links mTCP, which is GPLv3. The FreeDOS boot sector in src/boot/freedos is vendored unmodified under its own GPLv2-or-later license (its COPYING). Disk images you build hold other people’s software (FreeDOS, mTCP, and Turbo C from your own floppies): don’t redistribute an image with Turbo C on it.

ClawDOS stands on mTCP, FreeDOS, Open Watcom, the PicoMEM, 86Box and DOSBox-X.

headline: Show HN: Bootstrapping a compiler with AI run on to ARM64, WASM, SPIR-V
content:
Drake's question: C was built from B, B from something older. If every old tool added mistakes or waste, I would inherit all of it. So this folder grows a toolchain from a few hundred hand-written bytes, step by step, with the existing C compiler and the GNU tools used only as a referee that checks the answers, never as a builder.

The current completeness audit (implemented areas, open compiler work, and what is blocked on a decision or an external store) is docs/one_layer/OM_COMPLETION.md.

The scalar OSC IR backends are wasm/irwasm.om (WebAssembly MVP) and spirv/irspirv.om (SPIR-V 1.0 OpenCL Kernel). Both are compiled by seeded omc. IR mode casts (TYPE value) read the operand at its own type and convert it, the same as the AArch64 path, so ret ulong sub c 48 with c a uchar compiles. A bare number in the cast is range-checked against the cast's type (error 8) and a bool converts to or from a number only by comparison (error 9). seed/omc/gate-ir.sh pins 21 cast units against the C oracle plus 6 cast refusals; reverting the operand read to the cast's type makes the gate fail.

See SPIR-V usage, CPU parity gate and OpenCL demo.

To rebuild omc from the 408-byte seed on your own AArch64 Linux machine and check every rung against published hashes without touching tracked files, run sh seed/challenge/run.sh (see the seed-chain bootstrap challenge).

At commit e5b32567 (2026-10-27) the compiler source omc/omc.om is 12,040 lines and 208,168 bytes (sha256 7703da00055fc0c7a91fcae43071df76a3f277dbe867cb284a3bdff3bedb7e1b), and out/omc is 325,524 bytes. The line, function and byte counts given in each rung section below were recorded when that rung landed and are not current sizes.

Think of it as a ladder. Each rung is a small program, written in the language the rung below understands, and built by the rung below. Every rung must rebuild itself to the exact same bytes, which proves it reads its own language the same way the rung below does.

The only source for instruction bits is the public Arm Architecture Reference Manual (Arm document DDI 0487, revision M.d, sha256 80d589a4...e3d5). Every instruction in every hand-written file names the manual section it came from.

rung3/om3.s: a translator from Omegese (the small program language the model writes, see docs/one_layer/OMEGESE.md) to machine words. It is 1,486 instructions written in asm2's language and built by asm2 (7,092 bytes, rung3/om3.bin). rung3/table3.s2 adds 5 instruction lines to asm2's table, each naming its manual section.

What it reads: one Omegese function. What it writes: that function's machine words, ready to be called the same way the existing C compiler's output is called (same rules for inputs, result and errors).

The subset grew to what the 10 public practice tasks actually use: all nine number types, if/else, while with a limit, for, return, and add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder, and/or/xor, shifts, comparisons, negate, not, and type conversions, each with the same error stops ("traps") as the C path: overflow of a signed number, division by zero, a loop that runs past its limit, a conversion that does not fit, a shift that is too far. It refuses, with its own error number, what the tasks do not use (signed division, calls, arrays, more than one function).

How it builds code: every name gets its own register for as long as it exists. The C path keeps every value in memory and loads and stores it around each step (that is its documented design, OSC-1 design section 7, "no register allocation"), so a difference in word counts below measures that choice.

Checks (rung3/gate3.sh, results in build/seed/r3/evidence/, compared with the recorded receipt evidence/SEED-0/rung3/, never written over it):

Words of machine code per task (counts only, no timing; evidence/SEED-0/rung3/words.tsv):

Said plainly: the seed chain uses fewer words on every task, 164 against 600 in total (27%). Most of the gap is the C path's chosen design (every value goes to memory and back, see above), not a defect carried down from older tools.

many functions, and a names pass so a call may name any function in the unit, earlier or later (a later function is a call, never a new scalar). Program mode may recurse mutually. Function mode refuses a call cycle, including a function calling itself, as error 9;

whole programs: a source with fn main comes out as a complete Linux program, file header laid out by hand, no linker; it runs, reads its input, writes its output and exits;

fixed pools (global): memory for the source text, the tables and the output, sized when the program is translated. There is no heap at all, by Drake's rule 24;

local arrays (new), array inputs to functions (view read-only, edit writable), get, put, len; every array carries its length and every index is checked. There is no free: nothing is ever given back by hand (rule 24); fm7 and fm8, shared with the C path whose language needs free, are given to om4 without their free lines;

text: a fixed piece of bytes (an error message, the keyword list), stored with its length;

read, write, exit: the three Linux calls a compiler needs (stdin in, stdout out, a status);

signed divide, remainder and shift, true/false, for with a computed count, note lines. The exact meaning of every new word, and which check tests it, is in docs/one_layer/OMEGESE.md section 9.

Born from the seed, not from C: make omega-from-seed (or sh seed/omega-from-seed.sh) turns the hand-written seed0.hex into seed0 with the one named outside step (load0.sh, POSIX printf), then seed0 builds hex1, hex1 builds asm2, asm2 builds om4, om4 builds omc, and omc builds itself twice. The two self-builds must be the same bytes. The compiler is left at seed/out/omc, with its sha256 beside it. That file is the Omega compiler. Nothing in that path is C.

omc/omc.om: the compiler itself, written in Omegese, using only words om4 understands. It reads a program on its input and writes a ready-to-run Linux program (or, without fn main, bare machine words) on its output, with the file header laid out by hand and no linker. 3,212 lines, 125 functions. omc/genkw.awk once wrote the keyword chain into omc.om; the committed omc.om is the source, and the generator now lists every keyword (including host words 100-134) and packs 64-bit words exactly with decimal string arithmetic (verified against the chain: 0 mismatches). and the seed path does not run awk.

It is meant to do exactly what om4 does, word for word: the same machine words, the same error numbers, on the same line. That is on purpose: om4 then becomes a strict referee for omc, because any difference at all is a mistake. It is checked on every input listed below, not on every possible one.

How it is built: om4 translates omc.om into a program (stage 1, 76,748 bytes). Stage 1 then translates omc.om again (stage 2), and stage 2 translates it a third time (stage 3).

The few places where the language shaped the design:

Historical R5 checks (omc/gate5.sh, retained results in evidence/SEED-0/omc/), 177 cases, all pass:

Historical R5 size and speed (size.tsv, size-history.tsv, omc-words.tsv, compile-time.tsv in evidence/SEED-0/omc/; these receipts are immutable):

Current omc/gate5.sh writes disposable results to build/seed/r5/evidence/, never over historical receipts. seed/omc/size-history.tsv is the living measured-size ledger, initially copied byte for byte from the historical ledger. Before qualifying a compiler change, append its observed source line/function counts, emitted word count and compiler SHA-256. The gate checks that the last row names its independently rebuilt stage2; missing, empty or stale ledgers fail. It never updates its own prerequisite. Keep durable runs under a new evidence directory.

Current size reporting measures the complete compiler only. Compiling incomplete source prefixes is not a valid per-function measurement in a compiler with forward references; that old diagnostic was removed. All parent, C-referee, wrong-word-mutant, fuzz and refusal checks remain mandatory.

The branch-range gate is seeded .om, including its coordinator, generator, source mutator and decoder-output checker. See seed/qualification/security673/README.md for reconstruction. The compiler accepts the exact forward maximum and refuses larger conditional branches before emitting an executable. Direct probes of the actual encoder cover both signed extrema and misalignment; a local-array fixture exercises the current backward caller. GNU objdump independently decodes accepted forward branches and catches a deliberately weakened limit. Malformed-output controls and supervisor failures are separate from compiler correctness. Corrected evidence is in evidence/SECURITY-673/correction1/; earlier evidence is historical.

Limits, said plainly: omc has om4's limits, because it copies om4 (names up to 8 characters, 16 registers per function, values nested up to 1,024 deep, 8 MiB of input).

om4 does not learn structs. It remains the parent that rebuilds omc, and omc.om does not use the new words, so the two parents still build the same compiler. A struct program is a stack of 8-byte cells, given back when the function returns. There is no free.

Structs and the native host extension were built on separate branches from R5. They are now one compiler: seed/omc/omc.om, 4,616 lines and 173 functions, accepts both. The keyword table keeps both islands with no id shared (struct 85; host words 100 to 131).

Section 3 listed both words while the compiler refused them (keyword 77). omc now implements them (86 and 87) with the following semantics, and seed/omc/gate7.sh checks each one (11 cases plus the om4 refusal); seed/host/check.sh runs gate7.

fix/seed-ir-trap added a leading ir line that writes OSC IR version 1 for one function instead of AArch64 words. It branched from R6, so it lacked the native host words and break/trap. It is now part of the same compiler: seed/omc/omc.om, 5,395 lines and 209 functions, sha256 2b029a217e8f2d033b484dec3a5a24570370b8a139157f4204358e226d1e5bd9 (149,904 bytes).

IEEE-754 binary32 and binary64 are now part of the language, written in omc (f32, f64, bitcast, decimal literals, arithmetic, comparisons and conversions). A float value is its bit pattern in an ordinary integer register; arithmetic moves it to v0/v1, runs one scalar FP instruction and moves it back, with FPCR untouched and no fused operation.

The design says brackets are optional and separate words; the lexer did not implement that, so (5) was read as one unknown name. tok2 now emits ( and ) as one-character tokens even when they touch a value, and the existing group path returns the inner value with no code.

The first float slice converted N * 10^p only while both factors fit u64 (scale at most 18). The converter now keeps a normalized 64-bit significand, a binary exponent and one sticky bit (fmul10/fdiv10), rounds once to nearest even (froundsh) and packs with subnormal handling (fpack). No 128-bit integer and no double rounding are needed.

sizeof T / sizeof S and offsetof S f are compile-time constants of type ulong over the same 8-byte-cell layout that new/get/put use. They add no code and compose in expressions, which is the primitive that structure formats and the future C ABI work need in order to describe a layout without hard-coded numbers.

The first float slice spelled its words bits, sqrt, abs, min and max. Auditing the 103 .om files of the benchmark corpus against the pinned compiler (e5d60db8…) showed seven refusals: existing code uses bits as a parameter or variable in six files and min in one. A keyword may not take a name that existing code uses, so the float words are now bitcast, fsqrt, fabs, fmin, fmax (ids unchanged).

break had no counterpart. continue now finds the innermost loop like break, but its branch is patched to the loop's latch instead of its exit: the head of a while, so the condition and the hidden bound count run again, or the increment of a for, so the counter still advances. It uses the same fixup discipline (recorded with the loop's block index, patched when that loop closes, then marked spent) and the same 1024-site limit per function.

The current compiler was checked against the benchmark-pinned compiler over the real benchmark workspace, not just this repository's fixtures:

Method and per-scope counts: evidence/SEED-0/benchmark-parity/README.md. The corpus is external, so this is evidence rather than a gate.

IR mode used to consume non-fn top-level tokens and silently skip them, so a struct, global or text declaration simply vanished from the IR. ir_run now classifies every top-level token: blank lines and note lines are skipped, fn goes through the IR path, a struct/global/text declaration is error 9, and any other token is error 16. Nothing is lowered by accident.

random A off n flags fills a writable uchar slice from Linux getrandom through the same host-word path as the other slice operations: off/n are bounds-checked (trap 3), a view or text is refused (error 20), and flags is a typed int. It returns the bytes written or -errno; unknown flags return -EINVAL.

envcnt and envread index A off capacity read the process's own environment vector, which the start code preserves in X27 beside argv. envp[0] sits at X27 + 8*(argc+2); envread walks the entries before the requested index, so an index at or past the count traps 3. The slice rules match argread: bounds trap 3, a view/text is refused (error 20), and a short buffer returns -105 without modifying it.

chdir A off n changes the working directory through the same checked-path machinery as open/unlink/mkdir/rmdir: length-delimited path, private NUL-terminated copy, bounds trap 3, nonempty/embedded-zero refused, result 0 or -errno. The *at words leave AT_FDCWD in X0; chdir moves the path into X0 before syscall 49.

OMEGESE 9.6 states where the compiler runs out of room. seed/omc/gate12.sh now generates each boundary and checks both sides:

seed/host/check.sh runs gate12. Compiler unchanged since R19: 6,474 lines, 238 functions, sha256 7e7b68fd8922284e4b535005aef40b179bca70d8f3e775d7862af8c62c57e382.

seed/omc/gate13.sh embeds two deterministic generators (an explicit 16-bit LCG, never rand()):

The 600 programs run in about two seconds and seed/host/check.sh runs the gate.

ftrunc fd length sets an open descriptor's length through the scalar host path (Linux ftruncate, syscall 46). fd is int, length is long, and the result is long: 0 or minus the kernel error.

seed/omc/gate14.sh runs 35 programs whose expected exit statuses were computed exactly in Wolfram Language through the Wolfram MCP server (2026-10-23; server 2026.09.15), not by this compiler. The expressions and the returned table are in evidence/SEED-0/num-conformance/wolfram.txt.

Values are compared as main's value mod 256; traps must exit 100 + code. The gate runs in about 0.1 s and seed/host/check.sh runs it. Compiler unchanged: 6,480 lines, 238 functions, sha256 4aa1b0bf….

stat A off n B off capacity returns metadata for a checked path without opening it: Linux newfstatat with AT_FDCWD (syscall 79), writing the same 128-byte ARM64 structure as fstat. It returns 0 or minus the kernel error. The output slice must hold 128 bytes; a shorter one traps 3 before the kernel writes anything.

link A off n and symlnk A off n create a hard link or a symbolic link from a packed two-path list, reusing the renames/execprog list format: little-endian u16 count, then per record a u16 length and the bytes. The count must be 2, both records nonempty, the packet at most 4096 bytes. They call linkat (syscall 37) and symlinkat (36) and return 0 or minus the kernel error.

chmod A off n mode sets permissions on a checked path through fchmodat (syscall 53, flags 0). It reuses the path-copy machinery and the one-int argument shape of makedir; it returns 0 or minus the kernel error.

faccess A off n mode checks a checked path through faccessat (syscall 48, flags 0); mode is F_OK 0, X_OK 1, W_OK 2, R_OK 4. getuid, geteuid, getgid and getegid are zero-argument words (syscalls 174-177) returning the process's real and effective ids.

lstat A off n B off capacity writes the same 128-byte ARM64 stat structure as stat, but passes AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW (256) to newfstatat, so a final symbolic link is reported instead of followed. It returns 0 or minus the kernel error; a short output traps 3.

truncate A off n length sets a checked path's length through Linux truncate (syscall 45). It reuses the path-copy machinery; the length is a long, and after the copy the path moves to X0 and the length to X1.

seed/omc/gate15.sh pins the compiler's refusal table. At R30 that was one minimal program per code 3..23, each of which had to exit with exactly that code and print error N, plus a valid control. Since #797 the codes live in one registry, seed/omc/error-codes.reg, and gate15 covers every emitted code 1..25 and 27..30 (33 cases, each checked against its exact omc: line L: error C) and runs the seed/omc/codereg.om drift check with three negative controls; see OMEGESE §9.14.

chown A off n uid gid sets ownership on a checked path through fchownat (syscall 54, flags 0). It reuses the open-path argument shape (path plus two int ids); -1 leaves that id unchanged.

const NAME TYPE INTEGER at top level defines a typed value before use. It is visible to later functions, composes wherever a value goes (including call arguments), cannot be assigned (error 7), and is kept across function scope resets by advancing the global-name watermark. Integer types only; f32/f64 constants and IR mode are refused (error 9). Names are at most 8 characters and may not collide with a visible name, function or struct (error 10); the value must fit (error 8).

lenval accepts either a number or an integer constant name wherever an array length is parsed: local new, global pools, and view/edit parameter declarations. A name that is not an integer constant is error 16, and arrlen keeps the 1..16777216 range (errors 8 and 23). namescan now scans const lines before function signatures, so a signature may use a previously defined constant; the scan resets the global-name watermark afterwards so the body pass re-registers it.

const now accepts a float literal (f64 0.1, f32 0.1): rdval reads the float token, fspan converts it to target bits, and the name stores the bits with the float type. An integer literal under a float type (f64 5) is refused (error 16). Integer constants are also accepted as struct field lengths (1..64; over that is error 14), while a float constant used as any length is error 16.

trap N and while ... bound N now accept an integer constant as well as a literal (ranges 1..14 and 1..999999); a for count was already an ordinary value, so a constant works there too. A float constant is error 16 and an out-of-range integer keeps error 8.

IR mode now accepts top-level integer constants and folds each use to the same IR literal: the gate compiles const N uint 5 with ret N and the literal ret uint 5 form and requires byte-identical IR. Float constants in IR are still refused (error 9), as are struct/global/text declarations. ir_name consults the global name table only after failing to find an IR-local name, so locals still shadow as before.

fchdir fd changes the working directory to an open directory descriptor (syscall 50); getppid returns the parent process id (110); umask mask sets the file-mode mask and returns the previous one (166). All use the scalar host path; fd and mask are int, results are long.

fdsync fd syncs file data only (fdatasync, syscall 83). memfd A off n flags creates an anonymous in-memory file (memfd_create, syscall 279) and returns its descriptor; the slice is a name, copied privately like a path. Both are ordinary host words.

headline: Baseten Releases Bison-1 and Groundhog-1, Topping Decision Model Index
content:
Baseten has released bison-1 and groundhog-1, 2 open-weight decision models built on Google’s Gemma 4. Decision models do not write text. They return calibrated probabilities for yes/no, choice and score questions. The Baseten bison-1 decision model scores 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1. That ranks #1 of 19. Both models raise context from 16k to 128k tokens and accept images. For routing, triage and guardrail pipelines, that means full policies and histories in one call.

bison-1 is a 31B decision model from Baseten that post-trains Gemma 4 31B to return calibrated probabilities. groundhog-1 is the cheaper sibling. It fine-tunes Gemma 4 26B-A4B, a mixture-of-experts model with about 4B active parameters per token.

Both join Baseten’s existing lineup: mammoth-1 (27B), elephant-1 (9B) and joey-1 (2B). Those 3 sit on Qwen backbones. The new pair is Baseten’s first on what it calls an American backbone.

A request carries 1 state and any number of questions. The state is text, optionally with images. Each question has a type: noul (yes/no), choice (named options) or score (ordered levels).

The model answers every question in a single prefill pass. It returns P(yes), or the chosen option with a probabilities field. No output tokens are generated. Baseten’s earlier launch post lists ticket triage, spam detection, jailbreak guardrails and LLM routing as target tasks.

Requests longer than the trained limit are refused, not truncated. Pipelines that assume silent truncation will need a length check.

Baseten credits two sources: the Gemma base and more “soft labels” in the training mix. Soft labels use probability targets instead of 1 fixed correct answer. The model learns to report uncertainty that tracks how often it is right.

The result is a Brier score of 0.14, the lowest on the index. Baseten puts d1.2-ultra at 0.15. Lower is better.

On AA Decision Index v2.1, bison-1 scores 76. Liquid AI’s d1.2-ultra scores 75 and mammoth-1 scores 71. The index blends 6 evaluations, led by AA-Paperclip at 30%.

The bison-1 model card breaks out each component:

bison-1 ranks first on 4 of 6 components. Knowledge-heavy decisions are its weak spot.

On long context, Baseten reports LongMemEval M (128k) of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1. LongMemEval S reads 87.1 and 79.3. groundhog-1 has no official index score yet. Baseten expects it to match mammoth-1.

Both models are live on Baseten Model APIs. They use the same API as the older decision models, so switching means changing 1 model name. The IDs are decision-models/baseten-bison-latest and decision-models/baseten-groundhog-latest.

Pricing mirrors the older pair. bison-1 costs $0.10 per 1M tokens, like mammoth-1. groundhog-1 costs $0.035, like elephant-1. The bison-1 library page lists that as an input price, since no output tokens are produced.

Open BF16 weights sit on Hugging Face. Baseten lists no inference GPU or quantized builds. Training used 192 B200 GPUs for bison-1 and 128 for groundhog-1.

Check out the launch post, the bison-1 and groundhog-1 model cards, and the Baseten docs. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

headline: Riemann Hypothesis solved? Rethink math. Education. And the meaning of life
content:
Today, Levent Alpöge released a Lean proof of perhaps the most famous research problem in mathematics: the Riemann Hypothesis. This is completely different from the “hallucinatory” math that people may have seen from chats with AI.

Lean is a programming language for expressing math proofs, in a way that can be mechanically checked. Math is about precise logic: if A implies B, and B implies C, then A implies C. Not just sometimes. Always. Sort of like how computers have machine language: zeros and ones which express precise instructions to be executed faithfully. Talking to a computer in machine code is impossibly cumbersome for a human, just like if you had to tell your kid exactly what to do in the finest possible detail, down to when to breathe and how. Similarly, mathematicians never wrote down all of the detailed steps for mechanical checking their proofs, because that task was just too gargantuan for a human to do. Lean serves as a middle ground between human language and nitpicky logic, just like C++ is a middle ground that people can write, which a compiler turns into machine code. Analogously, there are (multiple) other programs (not large language models or generative AI) that compile the Lean code and check that every assertion in the proof is correct.

What that means is: as long as the statement is the real Riemann Hypothesis (it uses the standard library’s definition) and there are no bugs in the Lean verifiers, this is actually a proof. (By the way, there have been bugs in human verification of math research papers, which even got past the peer-review and publication process.)

That would be a big deal. I downloaded the Lean code myself to take a look. It extracts to 1 Gigabyte of text (more than 15 million lines of code) that looks like this:

Levent said that when he had Claude write the proof out in English, it ran past 250,000 pages.

It is impossible for any single human being to fully understand and check this volume of math in their lifetime. Your computer, however, has a processor which runs at gigahertz clock speed. “Giga” means 1 billion, and it’s notably the same order of magnitude as the length of the Lean proof. Ever since I was a kid, I was fascinated by the fact that a computer could do routine logic and arithmetic operations roughly a billion times faster than any human, and remember an amount of data roughly a billion times greater than any human. We’ve entered the age where this ability now extends from routine tasks to very much non-routine tasks.

I have too many suggestions to share, so I’ll spread them out over subsequent newsletters. I’ll focus on a few key points here.

As I wrote in poshenloh.com/posts/20260919-math-ai, there is not a single example of a species which has ever handed control to a less capable one. Levent wrote “... Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” Today, this is about pure math. Tomorrow, AI will be able to weave between the laws of physics and construct superweapons. When Sputnik flew over America, everyone worried about what the “other side” would do if they used their technological advantage to bend the world to their will. Every time I see an AI breakthrough, I think: we (humans) need to up our game to keep pace. What would you do if one day your adversary (whether human or AI) hacks the AI you have been using as your crutch? You need to have your own independent strong capabilities. Our human civilization also needs to have our own experts who bridge the gap between the math and technological frontier, and what humanity really needs and cares about. In order to do that, mathematicians must love humanity, and also be deeply curious about the breadth of the human experience. That is why I personally travel all over the world, teaching kids. I was in Lagos last month, New York City this week, and will be in Manila on Sunday.

Most people today feel powerless facing the enormity of the challenge. My optimism comes from my work daily with people who actually care enough to try to save the world, and have the intense curiosity to stay on top of every new technological or philosophical development. This is our Thought Full movement. We actually have a solution that can scale up dynamically to cover the whole world. It’s too long to fit in this margin, so it’s on that website.

The existing evaluation metrics were designed to find people who would add value in the old system. I speak from the experience of running a new ecosystem (LIVE) which uses comprehensive interviewing and observation techniques to identify people who deeply love humanity and deeply love thinking, and then introduces them to each other to build strong trusted relationships. We ignore standardized exam scores, math contest scores, and grades, and just ask them questions until we’ve gotten past everything they’ve prepared and learned, and then find out how they invent solutions on the fly. All the while, searching for a deep-set love of humanity. In the end, even though we never checked for the traditional metrics of achievement, the people we picked usually ended up extraordinary on those metrics too. I recommend focusing extraordinarily hard on values: make sure kids love delighting other people and love thinking. The rest follows from those axioms. So we need to focus our education environments accordingly. And that’s why we built The Game which we just launched in last week’s newsletter.

“Is there going to be a great human-versus-robots war? The answer is, unfortunately, yes,” Loh said. “My goal is to make sure the humans win.”

headline: The Most Important Charts in AI Are Wrong
content:
tl;dr: Real world AI data shows capabilities that are impressive but also dramatically inferior to those projected by influential AI forecasts and benchmarks - the very same forecasts and benchmarks that point to imminent super-intelligence.

By next year, according to influential forecasts, AIs should be able to autonomously accomplish tasks that would take humans years.

The METR task horizon measures benchmark performance. Both extrapolations of it using ECI scores and forecasts such as the original AI 2027 scenario dramatically over-estimate the length of task an AI can accomplish on real-world research tasks.

New data from OpenAI and Google on how AI is actually used inside those companies contradicts this, finding that real world work is far messier with far shorter timeframes.

In addition, the gap between the real world and forecasts is growing larger all the time. At 80% success, OpenAI’s real world internal task horizon grew dramatically more slowly from June to October than the AI 2027 scenario or extrapolations of the METR chart predict.

None of this is to blame forecasters or the creators of benchmarks. We were all building models in the absence of real-world data. Now that real-world data does exist, it’s time to shift from being AI theorists to being AI empiricists.

This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

2. Reality is Messy. AI in the Real World is Far Less Capable

3. AI Improvement is Much, Much Slower than Forecast

6. What Does this Mean for RSI and Super-Intelligence?

7. An AI Transparency Agenda – Starting with Anthropic

Appendix 2. How Much Do the Uncertainties Matter?

For years, one of the clearest ways to communicate that AI was growing in capability exponentially and would imminently eclipse human intellect was a chart of how long a task an AI could accomplish, published by an AI evaluation organization called METR. The METR chart measures tasks in how long it would take a human to accomplish them. It looks at the length of tasks AI can accomplish with certain levels of likelihood, generally either 80% or 50%. Other famous charts of a forthcoming fast takeoff or AI singularity often index on this same concept and same data set. The initial AI 2027 report projects a singularity fairly soon, as do recent updates from the leaders of the AI Futures Project who produced it.

Real world data inside of OpenAI and Google demonstrates that these charts are wrong. They are badly misleading about the current capabilities of AI and about the future growth rate of those capabilities. The gap between the hypothetical forecasts and real-world data is growing wider every month.

METR, AI Futures, and other organizations I’ll mention here are full of competent, smart, dedicated, honest people. I’ve learned quite a bit from them. I consider them mission-oriented, focused on making a better world, and obviously intelligent. None of this is meant as an aspersion of any of those individuals. They’ve done the best they could to project the future at a time when we didn’t have empirical data. And in many cases they’ve been stunningly accurate in their predictions.

The thrust of this post is that we have more and more of that empirical data, which paints a very different story of the future. And given that, it’s time to update. Secondly, AI forecasters and evaluators have, in many cases, been hobbled by the inherent limitations of measuring AI by using offline data sets where performance can be mechanically judged as success or failure. That process itself creates a sort of selection bias in AI benchmarks towards more cut and dry tasks and away from the messiness of real-life work. Even in computer science. METR, to their credit, understands this gap and has been working to improve their benchmarks, including in a new report out today.

A need for transparency. One final note before we begin. You’ll observe here that my critique doesn’t use much, if any, Anthropic data. That’s because Anthropic has so far not released the detail and quality of data that OpenAI has (and that Google is starting to emulate). Indeed, while METR recently looked at internal Anthropic data and found that Anthropic’s AI models are accelerating AI progress, Anthropic forced METR to redact the most compelling evidence from that report. For a company that says it’s soon going to hit a threshold where AI doubles its pace of progress, that’s irresponsible. The most foundational safety policy in AI ought to be transparency. OpenAI has now set the bar for transparency. Google appears to be following. The responsible thing for Anthropic and other AI companies to do is to engage in a transparency “race to the top” – a race to publish the information that the general public needs in order to make independent evaluations of what’s happening in AI and where it’s headed.

Below is the classic METR task length chart, edited for readability. It shows an exponential increase in the length of task that AI can autonomously complete. The version I’m showing below is at 80% success rate for AI.

That’s on a logarithmic scale. What looks like a straight line is actually an exponential increase, from a time horizon of just a few seconds in early 2020 to 4 hours with Claude Mythos Preview in early 2026.

Others have observed a general rule of thumb: That using the ECI score of an AI (The Epoch Capabilities Index, a general ‘IQ’ score for AI) they could generally predict time horizon. Among the models in the METR benchmark sample, about five ECI points corresponded to a doubling of the time horizon at 80% success.

ECI scores have been rising steadily for years. And Anthropic claims that they’ve seen an acceleration of that pace through the use of AI itself. [The public record shows that Anthropic has accelerated, though much of that was Anthropic coming from behind to catch up to the AI frontier. After their own investigation, METR estimates that Anthropic’s internal capability index was rising 1.9× as fast after October 2025 and judged that AI-assisted research likely accounted for most of the acceleration by October 2026. Economists Alex Imas and Luis Garicano find that increased pace of spending and other inputs appears to explain much of the acceleration. Their analysis leaves open how much of the gain came from AI.]

Using Anthropic’s internal capability index, AECI, to estimate what length tasks AI can accomplish today, Benjamin Todd, the founder of AI safety org 80,000 Hours, posted this chart estimating that the most powerful AI models available can autonomously complete tasks that are 30 – 40 hours long.

Finally, in 2025, the leaders of the AI Futures Project, in their initial “AI 2027” Forecast, published a chart like the below, predicting that in their fast-takeoff coding scenario, on a METR-style software-task scale, AI models would be able to autonomously accomplish tasks that take months by now, and more than a year by the end of 2027. [They since updated these forecasts, which we’ll look at below.]

All of those charts are wrong, inasmuch as they attempt to portray the real world. They may be narrowly correct, in that they measure success on a certain benchmark. But that benchmark doesn’t measure actual use of AI on the most contentious task – improving AI itself. What’s more, the gap between benchmarks and the real world is growing larger, rapidly.

OpenAI opens the kimono. In September, OpenAI released a post on research acceleration inside the company, that, for the first time, showed us how successful AI was at accomplishing tasks of given lengths, month by month, from January through July. This was the first time we’d had such detailed data from inside an AI company. It was a revelation about the messiness of the real world. Having it month by month also allowed us to track progress within OpenAI. In the Gemini Argon release, Google DeepMind followed suit, with a very similar chart (though of only one time period). And then again in November, OpenAI released an update of their September data, with more detail, an updated methodology, and a longer time series.

What the OpenAI and Google data show is that on real world tasks inside an AI company, AI models are 80% successful in accomplishing tasks of around nine minutes at Google and an adjusted 16 minutes at OpenAI.

Note that the OpenAI number above is higher than they report, as we’ve adjusted for possible reduction in success rate because of researchers giving AI ambiguous or unsolvable tasks, as well as errors in the tools that AI itself uses. Appendix 2 discusses how much that uncertainty changes the answer. None of the overall conclusions change much.

Some of this was expected. METR themselves understood that the lengths of the tasks they consolidated into a benchmark were the length of time a generally skilled programmer would take, but that an expert in that particular field could often accomplish the task much more rapidly. The gap was estimated to be as much as 10x. And the AI 2027 authors, to their credit, were indexing off of METR-defined lengths and realized that there could very well be a significant gap between benchmark times and real world times. They said as much.

That said, the gaps above are not a mere ten-fold. At 80% success, ECI → METR estimates are 33× OpenAI’s internal task length and 41× Google’s. The original AI 2027 scenario over-estimates real world task lengths by more than 100x. These are very major discrepancies.

Of course, exponential change eats up discrepancies like this. A straight extrapolation of the earlier METR benchmark assumes that the length of task an AI can accomplish will keep doubling every few months. That’s connected to a design feature of the ECI metric: It’s designed to reflect exponential growth in capabilities. Under exponential growth, even a 100-fold difference is only 7 doublings. That could be just two years.

But the gap between hypothetical AI capabilities and real world AI capabilities here isn’t static. It grew dramatically from June to October at 80% success for both the ECI → METR frontier trend and the original AI 2027 scenario.

Compare the shape of Benjamin Todd’s graph to real-world usage at OpenAI and Google, and you see this clear divergence.

We can see a similar gap comparing the original AI 2027 forecast with real world observations.

How fast are these hypotheticals diverging from what we observe inside OpenAI? In the four months from June to October, the divergence between Todd’s chart and real world observations at 80% success roughly tripled. At that rate, over a full year, the gap between forecasts and reality would grow by a factor of 30. That is not a good sign.

The original 2025 forecast from AI 2027 / AI Futures Project grows in its over-estimation of AI capabilities by more or less the same amount. The gap grew from 37× to over 100x, again implying that on an annual basis the gap would grow by a factor of more than 25.

To their credit, the authors of the AI 2027 forecast haven’t stuck to their original model. They’ve updated as new data has come in. But their August 2026 revision shows a similar, if milder, pattern. In its three time-horizon paths, the central gap grows by about 1.2–1.3× from June to October. That’s roughly a doubling of the gap on an annualized pace. Far better than other forecasts, but still dramatically off, and becoming less and less accurate over time.

These are not subtle differences. I respect anyone brave enough to create a quantitative model of the future and stick their neck out by writing it down. I’ve done the same many times. And no one ever bats a thousand when forecasting the future. I’ve had some major misses.

When those misses happen – when reality diverges dramatically from your forecast – the key thing is to update. The set of people who do is much smaller, alas. But I’m optimistic here.

So real world AI task lengths are far below those of hypotheticals. Are they improving exponentially? This is a slightly more technical question: “Is ECI exponential in real-world impacts?”

In the September OpenAI release, the trend lines looked decidedly less than exponential. This new data points the other direction. In this longer data set, exponential growth fits best at both 50% and 80% success. That said, at 80%, a straight line and a sub-linear trend fit almost as well, so it’s too soon to say conclusively that real-world task lengths are growing exponentially, even though it now looks most likely.

At 50% success rate, the best fit to the real-world data across all eight months is exponential improvement over time, with a doubling of AI achievable task length every 3.9 months on the central estimate, which is similar to METR’s latest estimate.

At 80% success rate, the best fit on the central estimate is also exponential, implying a doubling time of 5.6 months, about 40% slower than the doubling pace at 50% success rate. The relative likelihood favors the exponential over a straight line by just 1.36 to 1. Exponential growth is now our working assumption, but not yet conclusive.

Does this mean that real-world impact is exponential as a function of ECI? On task length, it appears to be the case. But as we’ll see below, on a more concrete real-world measures, the trend looks somewhat less than exponential.

There’s a second issue lurking in this data, which is that not only do AI models perform worse in the messy real world than in metrics, but, as Nathan Witkin points out, AI models also seem to perform especially worse when there’s a demand for high reliability.

As we just saw, AI models have been improving the length of task they can accomplish at 50% likelihood faster than they have at 80% likelihood on the central estimates. And the case for exponential improvement of task length at 50% is also stronger.

ECI → METR estimates overshoot the internal task lengths by 23–25× at 50% success and by a somewhat higher ratio of 33–41× at 80% across the two labs. That implies that we’ll see an even wider gap between measures and the real world at higher reliability numbers, though this is, for now, an extrapolation.

This observation dovetails with something people observe in the real world: AI is an incredibly powerful tool, but must be steered, corrected, pointed, and re-pointed in the right direction. AI is much more capable than it is reliable.

That has implications for RSI and super-intelligence. To operate truly autonomously, AIs will need to have reliabilities in a range well over 90%. Certainly to autonomously self-improve, AIs would need to chain together long sequences of tasks. Even 99% success rate may not be sufficient.

We don’t have sufficient data to actually measure AI task length at 95% or 99% success rate but plausible extrapolations suggest it will be quite low.

[Note that these extrapolations are as plausible and consistent with other AI modeling as possible, but still not empirical. Future data will likely update them. ]

Using two different ways to model the real-world OpenAI and Google internal data, we can estimate task lengths at which AIs will achieve ever higher levels of reliability.

The duration bins in the charts below are measured. Above 80% success, the task lengths come from fitted curves.

The brown line on the chart above is a logistic fit, something commonly used in AI metrics, and in particular by both METR and ECI. It is (as we’ll see in a moment) brutal in the estimate of AI capabilities at high reliability rates. I’ve chosen to put in another fit, which is a straight line on a log curve, capped at the obvious ceiling of 100% success rate. This is not commonly used in AI modeling, but I frankly wanted to find a plausible fit that was more optimistic about AI capabilities here.

The black line is the geometric mean of those two functions, an attempt to strike a middle ground between the model most commonly used in AI simulations of this sort and the gentler one I’ve tried to fit. If we zoom in, we see a projected pattern like this.

For easier reading, the chart below shows the conclusions: In the real world, AIs might currently only achieve 99% success rates on tasks that would take a human a few seconds to a very small number of minutes.

When will AI reach high reliability? How long might it take to get to high reliability on much longer tasks? This is an important question and it’s worth projecting. That said, we have limited data, so for now any answer is highly speculative. If the March–October 2026 pace continued, and improvement kept slowing at higher reliability thresholds, the middle projection for October 2035 would reach about 70 days of human work at 90% success, 2.6 days at 95%, and 2.4 hours at 98%. Even holding the future growth rate fixed, the two fits put that last number anywhere from 36 minutes to 9.6 hours.

These are, again, very speculative numbers. They are not, however, numbers that point to short term runaway AI self-improvement to super-intelligence. To reach fully automated RSI, AI models will have to perform complex tasks that take humans days or weeks, at very high reliability rates, possibly well above the 98% we’ve used above. These projections suggest that it’s going to take many more years before AI is capable of that.

Is there an upper bound of impossible tasks? One important caveat here: In offline metrics, we often see that there’s a ceiling that any AI can score, because the evaluation itself contains questions or tasks that are flawed or impossible. It’s possible that some of the effect we’re seeing in the internal OpenAI and Google data is that researchers inside the company are giving AIs short tasks that are actually flawed in their definition, non-sensical, or impossible for other reasons. That doesn’t change the overall thrust of our conclusions, but can change the specific numbers. More on that in Appendix 2.

What does this tell us about AI self-acceleration, RSI, and the prospects for runaway super-intelligence?

First, the OpenAI data don’t show any clear acceleration of AI progress pace. They show a very clear acceleration of usage of AI within the company, as an input to their next products, but not a clear acceleration of results. OpenAI very helpfully breaks up their blog post, indeed, into an inputs section and an outputs section. Inputs are soaring. Outputs are rising somewhat.

Second, as I mentioned above, these numbers don’t suggest that AI is close to being able to truly autonomously improve itself without human involvement. That will require extremely high levels of reliability at task lengths of days or longer.

Third, this data gives us a way to quantify the strength of the AI self-improvement loop.

The AI Self-Improvement Loop Still Looks Too Weak

In my earlier post on this topic I discussed a model of self-sustaining AI self-improvement developed by Tom Cunningham and colleagues that indexed on a key variable: How much additional productivity did one gain from each point of ECI gained by an AI? This is a clever way to quantify the strength of the AI self-improvement loop. And as a reminder, what Cunningham and colleagues found was that at a threshold of about 15% greater productivity per point of ECI, self-improvement could become self-sustaining. That’s illustrated below.

Adjusting for findings in the clearest experiment of experimental productivity that we know of (improving the Stockfish chess engine), I get a threshold of 19% added productivity for RSI to be self-sustaining, but that’s close enough.

In my earlier post I looked at experiment pace inside of OpenAI. Over the last year, OpenAI researchers have been able to run more experiments per month per person. Experiments, of course, are how we make discoveries that improve AI. While they’re not the final output we want (AI improvement) they’re one of the best proxies we have. headline: Experts warn: Everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme
content:
Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”

Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”

What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.

“Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”

Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”

It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company.

Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said.

“Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”
