headline: AI R&D-relevant model capabilities are improving rapidly
content:
This post presents evidence from our capability evaluations of public models relevant to AI R&D acceleration, up to Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. We remain significantly uncertain about central questions, including (1) what capabilities are in practice necessary for drastic acceleration, and (2) how quickly relevant model capabilities are improving.

We think that current public evidence is insufficient to rule out drastic AI R&D acceleration in the next couple of years. By drastic AI R&D acceleration we mean a situation where capabilities improve so quickly that humans are no longer able to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems.

This overview summarizes our main takeaways and their relevant sections within the post.

1 Background describes our motivation and aims, and how our thinking about capability evaluations has changed since the release of the original time horizons paper.

2 Methodology describes the different task sets used throughout the post, changes to human baselining methodology, and introduces our use of multiple score thresholds per task.

Figure 1: November 2026 update on AI capability measurement

3 Results contains the evidence for our main takeaways, which are:

4 Robustness details various checks we did on our results, such as checking for reward hacking and refusals. We also investigate the effectiveness of agent swarms as an elicitation technique and find that they seem helpful on verifiable tasks with a clear metric and fast feedback (compared to best-of-k⁠5), and have unclear or negative effects on our other tasks.

5 Discussion describes open questions for assessing AI R&D acceleration.

The appendices give more detail on our methodology, report robustness checks for our analyses, and highlight individual tasks with notable model behavior.

In this post we focus on the measurement of capabilities relevant to accelerating AI R&D. A particularly salient uncertainty for AI R&D relevant capability evaluation is whether strong performance on ‘well-specified’ tasks alone is sufficient for drastic AI R&D acceleration, or whether other capabilities are needed. We aim to present evidence that is informative regardless of the reader’s view on this question.

Historically, METR used our ‘time horizon’ metric as a way to measure the SWE-related agentic capabilities of AI systems.⁠6 Time horizon measurements were useful for risk assessments because (1) We considered the capabilities we were measuring with our time horizon suite to be necessary to pose catastrophic risk, (2) Our time horizon measurements were substantially grounded in human reference data, which made it easier to relate to risk relevant thresholds, and (3) measured capabilities were far from possible danger, which allowed us to argue these systems posed negligible catastrophic risk with reasonable confidence. For example, see METR’s evaluation of GPT-5.

Much has changed since the original release of time horizon, and this has led to various changes in our approach and thinking:

These changes in the landscape have led to various modifications in our approach to capability evaluation. In summary:

We discuss results from several tasks and experiments, many of which have their own specific methods, budgets, and affordances (e.g., GPUs, internet access, etc.). This section describes shared methodology.

Agent Setup. For all tasks, we evaluated models using our standard ReAct-style scaffold which amongst other tools, has bash, python and image-viewing tools.⁠17 We run models with xhigh or higher reasoning effort (a setting that controls how much the model reasons before acting), and the highest available reasoning setting for models older than Feb 2026. Token and time limits were chosen per task with the aim that agent performance reached a plateau in further inference scaling, though this aim wasn’t always achieved, see Appendix I: Inference Scaling for token scaling curves.

Task Suites. Our results cover three distinct task suites:

Figure 2: TH2 tasks are harder for AI agents and estimated to take humans longer

New tasks sets. The tasks we created sets span two kinds:

The table below summarizes the family of tasks in each set.

Scoring. Unlike our earlier suites, TH2 includes some tasks that are manually graded by humans (Making METR Tasks) or model judges (Investigate Wiki Incident).⁠21 In Time Horizon 1.1, continuously scored tasks are binarized via a task-specific threshold chosen to represent human performance. For our new tasks, where possible, we instead use multiple score thresholds based on intermediate human performance on the task. We define these thresholds as (score, time) points: each point is the time taken by an expert human to reach a corresponding score.

We defined (score, time) points for 34 of the 36 new tasks using a mix of successful human baselines (3 tasks) and researcher estimates of score given time (31 tasks). Despite our best efforts to recruit strong human baseliners, sometimes our baselines fell short of what we estimated an AI R&D expert (e.g., lab employee) could achieve. In such cases, we used our estimates when we could make reasonable arguments for their feasibility. Our estimates usually draw on records of real human work, e.g., NanoGPT speedrun records, and in some cases experts or our own experience. Where a task had more than one baseline, we used the points of the highest-scoring baseline. See Appendix A: Difficulty Estimation and Baselining for more details. We include robustness checks on how sensitive the time horizon trends are to our estimates in Appendix B: Time Horizon Diagnostics.

Run coverage. On both TH1.1 and our new suite TH2 we typically ran 15 models: GPT-4o, o1, GPT-5, Opus 4.5, Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8, Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Opus 5, Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5. Where we refer to using the MirrorCode suite of tasks, we use older runs that do not cover the latest models.⁠22

Lastly, in this post we use an IRT methodology to summarize agent performance on a single scale and deal with uneven run coverage. We describe this methodology next.

In some parts of our analyses, we want a common scale for model capabilities and task difficulties. Even though the capability profile of models is often ‘jagged’ compared to the human capability profile, model capability profiles are usually quite similar between models. This presents us with an opportunity to roughly summarize their capabilities with a single latent factor. Item Response Theory (IRT) models are one way to fit data to find these latent ‘strength’ factors. The METR Capability Index (MCI) is an IRT model that is very similar in spirit to the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI). However, unlike the ECI, which aggregates model performance across public benchmarks, our model treats the individual task as its unit of analysis and uses tasks we developed ourselves.

Notably, unlike a ‘time horizon’-like axis, IRT models do not require calibration against human performance. The ability axis reflects models’ patterns of strengths and weaknesses across tasks, rather than those of humans.

For each of our tasks, we define a scale in [0,1], where 0 corresponds to failure and 1 corresponds to full score⁠23, and fit a two parameter logistic for the score an agent \(m\) will get on a task \(t\)⁠:

\[p_{mt}=\sigma (\alpha_{t}(\theta_{m}-\beta_{t})),\quad \sigma (x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\]

where \(p_{mt}\) is the expected score agent \(m\) will get on task \(t\)⁠, \(\alpha_{t}\) is the task discrimination, \(\beta_{t}\) is the task difficulty, and \(\theta_{m}\) is the agent ability. When an agent’s ability \(\theta_{m}\) is equal to a task’s difficulty \(\beta_{t}\)⁠, the agent is expected to achieve 50% of the maximum possible score. The slope parameter \(\alpha_{t}\) captures how quickly the expected score changes around that 50% point.

To fit this two-parameter logistic, we maximize the fractional-logit log-likelihood function. We also apply weightings to, for instance, upweight based on the number of runs we have on a task, downweight large numbers of similar tasks, and downweight ‘noisy’ tasks where our observed data is not well fit by our model. We generate 95% confidence intervals using hierarchical bootstrap across task families and runs. For full IRT model and fitting details, see Appendix C: MCI Modelling Methodology. We also do various robustness checks of our model, which can be found in Appendix E: MCI Robustness Checks.

In this section we’ll cover our results and other collected evidence. Section 3.A covers AI R&D relevant model capability strengths, Section 3.B covers model limitations, and Section 3.C covers capability trends.

We find that current public frontier models have extremely strong capabilities on optimization tasks, often outperforming skilled humans. Generally, these tasks have a clearly defined goal that is cheaply checkable. Usually the solution has few required criteria or constraints other than those expressed by some score, and often this score is observable to the agent.

Section 3.A.1 describes evidence that models outperform our humans on our hard but well-defined coding and optimization tasks. Section 3.A.2 describes model performance relative to top experts in places where we have the data to do so.

Appendix O: Qualitative and External Evidence on Models’ Strengths and Limitations also describes external evidence that model strengths in this area extend beyond just benchmarks.

We see strong performance from models on TH1.1, our old (primarily verifiable) sets of tasks, as well as on the verifiable portion of our TH2 tasks. Current public frontier models have an estimated time horizon of up to 27 hours on the verifiable subset of our TH2 tasks.

We also found that current public frontier models were able to beat the human baseliners that we recruited on the 3 tasks we attempted to acquire human baselines for. Since we want to measure whether models are able to replace AI developer employees, we aimed to acquire baseliners of a similar skill level. We recruited people with specialist knowledge in the task domain. For instance, for Train a Program our best external baseliner is a former International Grandmaster on Codeforces and won the 2020 Kaggle ARC-AGI competition. For Minecraft Bot and Reverse Conway, our best-performing baseliners were somewhat less credentialed, but had compensatory specialist knowledge or experience. We paid \$200-350/hr and spent a total of roughly \$90k for 7 attempted baselines.

Overall, we are uncertain about the comparability of our baseliners to AI R&D lab employees. We would guess that our baseliners’ skill within the task domain probably didn’t match the level of skill that typical frontier AI researchers have within their own domain. On the one hand, our baseliners were experienced, and often had specific experience relevant to the task. On the other hand, AI developers offer very high compensation, and have recruiting teams optimizing for finding highly talented individuals. Additionally, our tasks required dozens of hours of commitment, which plausibly selected against potential participants with full-time employment, and may have led to some adverse selection effects. For more details on human baselines see Appendix A: Difficulty Estimation and Baselining.

Various other work also observes high capability on these kinds of tasks. For instance, on MirrorCode, where agents reimplement software by checking against a full test suite, Opus 5.5 solves 77% of medium to large programs that would take human experts weeks to months to do on their own. GPT-6 Astra recently scored 98% on FrontierMath Tier 4, a benchmark of research-level math problems designed to take a strong mathematician specializing in that domain 1-2 weeks.

For two of our TH2 verifiable task families we have a larger pool of pre-existing human data to compare model performance against. On these two task families, we observe AI agents had high percentile performance but were generally unable to beat the very top performing humans.

Figure 3: Current public frontier models outperform most humans (but not always the very top experts) on tasks with a large pool of participants

On the left, we show where model solutions rank against human participants in AZsPCs contests. On the right, we show model’s speedup over record #78 ranked among speedups of human records #79 to #92. For AZsPCs, models had 48 hours on a 28-core machine, and participants had about three months. For Budget NanoGPT, models had 48 hours on 8xH100s, and contributors typically reported 16 to 40 hours per record.

The first of these two task families was 15 Al Zimmermann contests, multi-month long optimization competitions. We find the median placement of the strongest models (Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra) is the 96th to 98th percentile of human participants (97 to 413 participants per contest). We estimate that a dedicated human participant might spend between 90 hr and 180 hr over the course of the competition. We think the top of the human participant pool is quite strong.⁠24 In the median contest, roughly 4 humans beat the strongest models we tested, see Figure 3(a).

The second of these two task families was Budget NanoGPT speedrun, where we run the AI agent with a comparable amount of compute⁠25 to what human speedrunners typically use. Agent solutions (all starting from record #78) and human records aren't perfectly comparable, since each human record builds on previous records. However, interviews with contributors suggest that each human record took a similar amount of labor and resources, comparable to one of our agent runs. So we compare each agent run’s speedup to the speedup of individual human records, and believe this comparison is rough but still informative. Also note that recent "human records" can be AI-assisted (sometimes heavily so), and that we only include human records set up to Aug 2026.

On Budget NanoGPT speedrun, we find that fully autonomous AI agents outperform many competent speedrunners, achieving better speedups whilst costing less. However, top human contributors still can reach much larger speedups than AI agents, see Figure 3(b). The best AI agent run (of 2 to 5 runs per model) reached a 15.7% speedup over our starting record in 48 hours. The author of a recent unusually strong record (#92), with AI assistance for coding, estimated spending about 60 hours for a 41% speedup over the previous record.

For more detail on each of the results see Appendix K: Al Zimmermann's Programming Contests and Appendix L: Budget NanoGPT.

In this section we present evidence that current public frontier models have capability limitations that may prevent them from drastically accelerating AI R&D via automating research work.

In Section 3.B.1, we introduce Lifecycle Cost, a rough proxy for how costly a task would be to build and use as an RL training environment. We find that on our dataset, models perform worse on tasks with higher Lifecycle Cost, even when controlling for task length.

Section 3.B.2 describes evidence of limitations related to performing well on tasks where it is difficult to get clear empirical feedback about the quality of the solution. In these tasks, agents need to create their own metrics of quality, handle tradeoffs, or exercise judgment.

Appendix O: Qualitative and External Evidence on Models’ Strengths and Limitations also describes external evidence on weaknesses in the context of AI-related research.

As discussed in Section 1, the evals that are METR’s current primary way of measuring model capabilities are likely to have much in common with the RL environments that companies use to train their models. This is because both METR and AI developers want to be able to cheaply, easily capture signals about model capabilities. As RL has become a larger share of training, we have become more concerned that this overlap causes systematic measurement issues.

To try to quantify how difficult a task is to make into an RL environment, we created a very rough proxy measure which we call Lifecycle Cost. This is the cost for us to develop a containerized environment for the task, and then to run and score the task 100 times.⁠26 The goal with this quantity is not to reflect the ‘real cost’ of RL environments per se, but rather to have some rough quantitative metric of relative costliness.

Table 1 gives examples of properties that we have found make it more expensive to create highly realistic tasks, which Lifecycle Cost aims to capture.

Figure 4: Properties that make it more expensive to create realistic tasks

We estimate Lifecycle Cost for our tasks with an LLM judge (Opus 5.5). This judge is given the task code (including the README, instructions, and scoring), and asked to estimate various costs associated with the task like e.g. development, QA, and scoring costs. We also amortize shared development costs over families of similar tasks. We iterated on the prompt for the judge such that the judge’s estimates roughly matched our own for about 10 tasks across domains and cost ranges.⁠33 While we expect our prompt to generalize reasonably well to tasks outside ours, some choices like which phases we break cost into, how much we assume AI speeds up task development, labor rates, etc. reflect our own experience. For full details of how we estimate Lifecycle Cost see Appendix F: Estimating Lifecycle Cost for Tasks.

We think there are various limitations to Lifecycle Cost as a proxy for ‘difficulty to make a suitable RL environment’, and also to using ‘difficulty to make a suitable RL environment’ as a predictor of model performance broadly:

Figure 5 shows a scatter plot of human time-to-complete vs Lifecycle Cost for our tasks. For TH2 tasks, Lifecycle Cost is estimated only for the highest score threshold. On our dataset, human time-to-complete and Lifecycle Cost are quite correlated (R2 = 0.82).⁠34

Figure 5: Lifecycle costs are correlated with the estimated human completion times, for tasks in our dataset

When we control for this correlation between time-to-complete and Lifecycle Cost we find that (for a given length) tasks with higher Lifecycle Cost tend to be somewhat more difficult than what would be predicted by their time-to-complete alone (R2 = 0.14), see Figure 6.⁠35⁠36

Figure 6: Tasks we estimate would be costly to turn into RL environments tend to also be harder for models

However, our data is noisy and could be affected by a few things. For example, many of our task times are estimates, and if they are systematically wrong, part of this effect could come from error in task time. That said, it’s somewhat reassuring that when we use models to estimate task time instead of human estimates/baseline, we also observe a similar trend. Another reason could be that this effect is driven primarily by a few high cost tasks. In the plot above, we account for this by filtering such outlier tasks. More ablations are in Appendix F: Estimating Lifecycle Cost for Tasks.

When we subset our tasks by high and low Lifecycle Cost, controlling for task length, and plot time horizons over release dates, we find that models perform worse on the higher Lifecycle Cost subset of our tasks, see Figure 7. On average, the higher Lifecycle Cost subset is 2.9x as expensive as the lower Lifecycle Cost subset, and models perform 2.9x worse in terms of time horizon, equivalent to 1.5 doublings.

Interestingly, compared to the lower lifecycle cost subset, model performance on the higher lifecycle cost subset is closer to performance reported by OpenAI on their own internal research usage.⁠37 We don’t have many task distributions to compare here, but we think this is at least an encouraging sign about our ability to create evaluations that are directionally more predictive of performance on ‘actual’ AI R&D tasks. headline: Things I learned coding with AI for a year
content:
How I write software has changed dramatically over the last twelve months. It will probably change again in the next twelve, but I thought it might be helpful (to myself and others) if I wrote down some observations about how things have seemed to shake out in my day to day, and how I work now as a result.

This is probably the largest and most abstract observation, and despite sounding metaphorical, it isn’t. You set down basic rules and goals as a seed, see what sprouts out of them, and steer elements of the resulting code as it grows so that it does the things you want the way you want, without really worrying about the finer details.

I start every project with a constitution type document. It details why the codebase is being created, specific design principles and preferences it is to adhere to, specific technologies to use, and standing rules for what the development loop should look like.

When I first started using AI I had a natural inclination to frontload only concrete directives, but over time, as models have gotten better, I've noticed that having the "why" in the document really helps with aligning AI to my actual goals.

This is ultimately a living document that often becomes the README for the whole repo, but you need some solid content before you let an AI rip.

Even if the code generated is beautiful, well organized, well abstracted, and architected around the best possible principles, no one is going to read it directly. All codebases, big and small, beautiful and ugly, are inspected by proxy using AI to search and distill the contents as needed.

My top level README files lay out three things: purpose, structure, and use. These draw from the constitution document I mentioned before, and become more important over time, because AI will need to see this information at the start of each fresh session. Third party agents will want it as well.

Before AI, starting a new project meant having a very specific vision that you work toward for weeks or months, refining it as you go. You would typically have several weeks, or even months, of consistent effort, building context and a mental model around how things currently work and how the system should be expanded or changed over time.

This journey no longer exists. The system outgrows your ability to understand it completely in a matter of weeks, or even days. Collaborators are there the moment you create the git repo, in the form of AI agents. You no longer get the luxury of refining a vision for the system over time the same way.

However, you now get to try many different visions and throw them away very rapidly. Honestly, it's a lot better, and less prone to getting stuck in the horrible local minima most legacy systems wind up in.

I frequently task AI with exploring alternative designs or technologies applied existing systems.

"What if I wanted to separate search and discovery columns into a separate database?"

I will ask AI to plan a migration to a different architecture, different design patterns, different build systems, different CI providers, and so on, and see what comes out. I probably do this once every two weeks even though I almost never follow through (three times in nine months I have), because I almost always learn something from the plans themselves. Sometimes I discover something has been tightly coupled that shouldn't be, sometimes I find out a feature works differently than I expected, and sometimes I find a pretty big simplicity or performance win.

I’m not saying read every line of code and latch on to the fine details. I’m saying rules and conventions can make AI more or less efficient, and efficiency still matters. Getting the same result in less time with less headaches is better, full stop, and caring about design, conventions, and the order in which you attack functionality has a huge effect.

Learn design patterns. Learn what they are useful for and why they were invented. These things communicate principles in a compact and concise way and have very clear costs and benefits. The reasons they exist have not disappeared from the code, only from our view of it.

YAGNI as a concept has shifted from being something you apply to code to something you apply to your prompts. Ask an AI for one thing at a time, and be specific about what you want. DRY is more about structure than anything else. You need a codebase the AI can navigate and search coherently or it will rewrite the same functions over and over again in different places.

I work on a single unit of functionality at a time, and separate refactoring from functional changes, at least along commit boundaries.

I also adhere to strict structural rules in where code goes based on what it does, with both breadth and depth structures. “Domains” are the breadth structure and represent the kinds of “things” or “categories” a service or system handles or works on, like “users”, “trust providers”, or “tokens”. “Layers” are the depth structure, and break domains up into different responsibilities like persistence, telemetry, service handlers, or daemons. This allows me to give AI commands with semantic specificity that can translate directly into the directories and files affected without me naming specific paths, and keeps the AI from searching my entire codebase every time I ask it to complete a task.

History builds up in comments, files are copied instead of imported, and package dependencies becoming a directionless web. Code that is hard to navigate cause AI to write code that is hard to navigate. AI goes in without enough context, no way to gather relevant context, and as a result gives you less and less of what you want over time.

I add cleanup steps to all of my feature development loops. On some cadence, not necessarily every task, I task the AI with specific goals for code reduction, comment reduction, or decoupling, on the basis of simplification and single responsibility.

In my experience, most of what SOTA AI tends to “get wrong” stems from some missing piece of information. Either environment knowledge not in the codebase, preferences I didn’t write down, or a decision made in a previous session. Outside of the current context window, LLMs only know what they are trained on, and your codebase probably was not in that corpus. Certainly not prominently enough to meaningfully impact your experience.

I work in what I call “metaplans”. I start with some high level goals, and build out a file hierarchy of different pieces of the work needed to accomplish those goals in various levels of detail. Execution comes down to executing the “leaf” nodes, which are concrete code changes, of that file tree. The higher level goals, and all the intermediate decisions and discussions live on after those are complete. I keep the files around for a few weeks or more for future work to reference. This is especially helpful in other planning sessions, as prior decisions are often good context for AI to use when planning downstream features and functionality.

Probably as a mitigation for their blind spots, LLMs will look around way more than necessary, at things that have nothing to do with what you want, and once they have looked somewhere, they can become convinced that it is relevant, whether or not it is. This can often cause off-target changes.

I keep strict rules around how code is shared across services, repositories, and even within packages. Code is shared at the lowest level it can be, in “pkg” directories. Code shared between domains must live in a shared “pkg” directory. Code in a “pkg” directory must be stateless. It can name or handle state via interfaces and the like, but cannot hold state itself, as state always belongs to a domain. I have linters that enforce many rules like this to promote an easily searchable codebase.

LLMs are trained on A LOT of data. You can steer them well with their context window, but they are fundamentally limited to working with the patterns and concepts they are trained on.

No matter how many times you repeat “Do not leave code comments detailing code history” in your prompt, if the model was trained on a billion examples of historical comments, you are going to get them. The weights will always win.

Give up. Keep the rules you want there, maybe even add a cleanup loop to reinforce the behavior, but if the model ignores them, you just have to let it go. Pick your battles.

headline: Detecting AI Agents in Next.js with Vouched KYA
content:
Brandon Minnick, Developer Advocate · November 19, 2026

AI agents like ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity are already browsing websites on behalf of real people, and most of our websites can't tell them apart from humans or crawlers. But the good news is that we can fix that! In this post, we'll add Vouched KYA's Detect to a Next.js app in about 5 minutes, for free.

Prefer to watch? Here's the video walkthrough.

You've probably heard of KYC (Know Your Customer). Know Your Agent (KYA) is the same idea for the agent era: knowing which AI agents are interacting with our business, and which human authorized them. Vouched built Vouched KYA on KYA-OS, an open standard it has donated to the Decentralized Identity Foundation.

Vouched Detect classifies every request that reaches our servers as human, ai_agent, bot or incomplete_data. In Next.js, we run Vouched's detection engine right inside our app's Proxy, adding just a few milliseconds to each request. And - the best part - Detect has a free tier, no card required. Vouched KYA's paid plans add Enforce and Govern, where we can apply policies to agents and verify who authorized them. (We'll cover those in future posts!)

You can find the completed code sample here: https://github.com/vouched/KnowYourAgentWebsite-Nextjs-Sample

Our API key is a secret, so it should NEVER be committed to source control. Next.js loads environment variables from .env.local, and the .gitignore that create-next-app generates already ignores it. Be sure to double-check your .gitignore; your future-self will thank you 💯.

In the root of our project, create .env.local:

And when we deploy to production, be sure to set the same environment variable in our host, like Vercel.

Next.js runs proxy.ts before every request, which makes it the perfect place for Detect. Create proxy.ts in the root of our project, or in src/ if our app uses one:

And that's it! Just one function call and we're up and running.

withCheckpoint enforces policies by default, so in this example, we turn on observe mode explicitly. And if we forget our API key, our app still works; the SDK just can't report to our dashboard.

Our website looks exactly the same, and that's the point.

In a second terminal (on Windows PowerShell, type curl.exe instead of curl):

Among the response headers, we'll find these:

It works! Detect is running in observe mode, and Permit is what it would have done if it were enforcing. Within a minute, our request shows up in the Vouched KYA dashboard under Detect → Activity as an ai_agent named ChatGPT. 🎉 Not seeing it? Add debug: true to withCheckpoint, and the SDK logs why a report didn't reach Vouched, like a mistyped API key.

The dashboard labels it a bot, because it's a crawler collecting training data, not an AI assistant browsing on behalf of a person.

The SDK calls onResult after it classifies each request, the perfect place to log it, send it to our analytics, or save it to our database. Let's add it to proxy.ts:

Send the ChatGPT and GPTBot requests again, plus plain old curl -I http://localhost:3000/, and our terminal shows:

Vouched KYA even knows curl is a developer tool! One thing to know: the SDK waits for onResult before it responds, so for slow work, use after() to run it after the response is sent.

Because the engine runs inside our app, we can unit test proxy.ts with any user agent we like, no network required. The sample's Vitest tests do exactly that, with helpers that fake Vouched's API, so our CI catches any @kya-os/checkpoint-nextjs update that changes how our traffic is classified.

AI agents are already visiting our websites, and with @kya-os/checkpoint-nextjs, it only takes one function call (and zero dollars) to start seeing them.

The completed sample does everything in this post, plus one fun extra: paste your Project ID and API key into the page, click Send simulated traffic, and watch ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, GPTBot and more arrive in your dashboard!

Why "Would be blocked"? The sample adds engineConfig: { tier3Action: "block" }, which tells Vouched KYA to block known AI agents, AI crawlers and headless browsers. Our proxy.ts leaves it out, which is why ChatGPT got Permit. In observe mode, nothing gets blocked either way.

Building with .NET instead? Check out the Blazor Server sample.

Next, we'll move from observing to enforcing with Enforce. Subscribe to the Vouched KYA newsletter at the bottom of the Vouched KYA home page so you don't miss it!

headline: House China Cmte: China Trying to Get US Companies Addicted to Chinese AI Models
content:
Today, Chairman John Moolenaar (R-MI) of the House Select Committee on China and Chairman Andrew R. Garbarino (R-NY) of the House Committee on Homeland Security released a report following their joint investigation into the integration of Chinese-developed open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) models into American companies' consumer platforms. The joint investigation focused on the origin of these models, their data, training, potential for unauthorized distillation, and how companies around the world purchase and acquire them. The committees also evaluated the U.S. open-weight AI strategy, and if it sufficiently ensures American entities are not forced to choose between expensive or proprietary U.S. models and cheap, capable China-based alternatives.

The committees began this investigation in April 2026 with letters to Anysphere and Airbnb. Both companies have since engaged with the committees regarding the technical, commercial, and security considerations surrounding their evaluation and use of Chinese open-weight models. As a next step in the investigation, the Chairmen sent a letter to DoorDash requesting similar information in July 2026.

In the report, Chairmen Garbarino and Moolenaar write:

“The investigation uncovered risks that American businesses, policymakers, and national security officials can no longer afford to overlook or downplay. From Silicon Valley startups to Fortune 500 companies, American businesses are increasingly adopting PRC-developed open-weight models because they are inexpensive, customizable, and competitive with leading American systems. Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap.”

“Congress has too often been behind the curve on emerging technology. As one of our colleagues observed after a briefing on these issues, AI is advancing so quickly that Congress risks being ‘light years behind.’ With this investigation, we intend to narrow that gap. We should not wait five years to discover that much of the world, and much of the United States, runs on AI shaped by the CCP, leaving policymakers with little choice but another costly rip and replace effort. The time to act is now, while we still have the opportunity and leverage to do so."

The Committees’ investigation found that personnel associated with the 1st Bureau of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Cyberspace Force, the unit responsible for cyber espionage, and attacks have been present on multiple occasions at the Beijing headquarters of Zhipu, most recently in August 2026. These visits indicate a channel between the PLA’s cyber intelligence apparatus and one of China’s leading AI developers.

The Committees’ review of PLA procurement records also found the Chinese military building these models directly into its cyber operations. A July 2026 procurement for a large PLA cyber range, a system for generating “cybersecurity professional capability,” required integrating DeepSeek to support “intelligent attack” and “intelligent penetration.” Other records show a command information system built around Alibaba’s Qwen and DeepSeek, and a 2026 project requiring models from DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot, and MiniMax to run on a network cut off from the internet for military AI agent development. Documents produced to the Committees show that these same model families are running inside major American companies.

The new report comes as China has intensified its efforts to close the AI innovation gap with leading U.S. frontier labs through model distillation, intellectual property theft, and other illicit means. In September 2026, the National Security Agency (NSA), CISA, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released a joint advisory warning of the national security impacts of these large-scale distillation efforts against American AI companies, particularly as China utilizes advanced AI models to increase the scale, scope, and speed of its intrusions into U.S. systems.

headline: A push for a treaty to not allow AI total control over nukes
content:
Juan Manuel Santos and Denis Mukwege were honoured to participate in this week's Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on Nuclear Weapons and AI at the Vatican, where they signed the following declaration:

Adopted by the participants of the Global Nobel Laureates AssemblyBorgo Laudato Si', Vatican – July 2026

Humanity stands at a defining moment in its history.

More than eighty years after the dawn of the nuclear age, and at the threshold of the age of artificial intelligence, we are presented with an unprecedented challenge. Never before has scientific progress offered such extraordinary opportunities while simultaneously creating such profound risks to our common future.

When nuclear weapons were first being developed, the world had a chance to avoid living in a permanent dynamic of fear. We failed, and as a result, humanity has lived at the edge of nuclear annihilation.

With AI, a similar danger presents itself. AI built into nuclear systems leaves little time for, or even replaces, human judgement in a crisis. This technology changes the context in which nuclear-armed states compete with each other. AI will likely cause mass job loss and sharpen economic competition between nuclear-armed states. AI uplifts cyber attacks that can fracture critical civilian and strategic infrastructure. AI enables information warfare: Peace depends on a shared reality. Without facts there can be no truth; without truth there can be no trust; and without trust, no dialogue, no verification, and no restraint among nations.

The most advanced AI capabilities, computing resources, and data infrastructures are becoming increasingly concentrated in a small number of countries and corporations, creating significant asymmetries of power and limited incentives for cooperation. AI is a technology that causes economic, military, and social disruption, and is developing at a pace unprecedented in human history.In the midst of a worsening nuclear arms race, we are embarking on an equally dangerous AI race.

Pope Leo XIV, invoking values shared across religious traditions, has called humanity toward an "unarmed and disarming peace." We reject the belief that lasting security can be built on fear, domination, or the permanent threat of mutual destruction. Security cannot rest indefinitely upon the reality of mutual destruction.

Conscious of our shared responsibility toward present and future generations, we adopt the following principles:

We recognize that AI is an arena of strategic competition, like nuclear weapons before it. We call on governments, frontier AI developers, researchers and the international community to act now, through governance arrangements such as benefit-sharing mechanisms, the promotion of AI applications that serve human wellbeing, and restraint in its most destabilizing applications, to reduce these risks while the choice remains ours. We must disarm the next arms race, both AI and nuclear, before they define the next century as well.

AI developers should transparently publish the principles that guide the behavior of their models and be held responsible and liable for those models' adherence to such principles. AI should be developed and monitored to be in alignment with humanity’s interests, including international law and respect for human rights.

Furthermore, no organisation should initiate, and no government should permit, fully-automated recursive self-improvement in artificial intelligence systems without the means to monitor, and if needed, to halt such systems.

An automated system should never make the final decision to launch a nuclear weapon. We call for the adoption of an international treaty prohibiting the reckless integration of artificial intelligence into nuclear command, control, and launch systems so that meaningful human control is maintained.

We must prevent the malicious use of artificial intelligence in cyber operations and attacks against critical nuclear infrastructure. Nuclear states must engage in fail-safe reviews to reduce the vulnerability of their nuclear forces to unauthorized control or manipulation by AI.

We promote the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence to improve human well-being, accelerate scientific and medical progress, protect the environment, strengthen resilience, and advance peace, sustainable development, and the common good.

We call on governments, corporations, and international organizations to enable coordinated slowdown of frontier AI development by establishing shared mechanisms, such as verification and robust internal and external evaluations.

We support the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, and promotion of other efforts in the spirit of Magnifica Humanitas.

We call for expanded research and dialogue to propose new institutional pathways for international governance of AI and future implementation of global governance initiatives.

We recognize that the challenges we face will likely be solved by the next generation of leaders. Young people must be empowered to engage with nuclear, AI, and other potentially catastrophic threats, through education, mentorship, intergenerational partnership, and inclusive participation across all regions, cultures, and communities. We must advance education initiatives that foster ethical responsibility, critical thinking, media and AI literacy, and a culture of peace.

We acknowledge that humanity faces numerous connected threats, the unintended consequences of which often impact those who do not have access or control over such technologies. We call for a digital commons which grows data to advance understanding and action for nuclear weapons, ungoverned AI, and other existential threats.

We call for urgent, sustained, and good-faith negotiations leading, within an agreed and time-bound framework, to the verifiable and irreversible elimination of nuclear weapons. The international community must reject the normalization of nuclear weapons as permanent instruments of security and strengthen the humanitarian and legal norms embodied in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

We call on nuclear-armed states to halt renewed arms racing and the expansion of their arsenals, resume bilateral and multilateral negotiations on arms control and disarmament, and fulfill their obligations and commitments under international law. States should pursue verifiable restraints and reductions; lower alert levels; extend decision time; move away from launch-on-warning and prompt-retaliatory postures; reduce the role of nuclear weapons in security doctrines; strengthen crisis communications; prevent cyber operations against nuclear command, control, and communications; and build cooperation to prevent misunderstanding, miscalculation, and unintended escalation.

Nuclear nations must promote policies and doctrines that diminish the role of nuclear weapons, and reduce the likelihood of first use and catastrophic war.

Inspired by the words of Nobel Laureates Bertrand Russell and Albert Einstein, “We appeal as human beings to human beings: remember your humanity, and forget the rest.”

Our survival and the survival of future generations are at stake.

headline: If AI found better drugs for every disease, what would it cost to prove it?
content:
Getting new helpful medicines to patients is hard, and historically it’s been getting harder. From 1950 to 2010, the number of new approved drugs per billion dollars of R&D spending halved roughly every nine years. In 2012, Jack Scannell and colleagues called this Eroom’s law, or “Moore’s law backwards”.1 One theory that explains this is the “better than the Beatles” problem: we’ve already made substantial progress on various diseases, and statistically speaking, it requires more and more patients (and therefore more and more funding) to demonstrate marginal improvements — just like how the next generation of pop stars needs to compete with the Beatles catalogue.

Despite that progress, the global burden of disease is still enormous. Most positive visions of the future put forward by AI leaders today involve the use of AI to accelerate the eradication of this burden.2 But even if AI produces a miracle drug for every disease, we still need to run the clinical trials to prove that things are getting better.

Saloni Dattani recently made a fun game to help illustrate the challenges in running these sorts of clinical trials.3 My main takeaway is that making trials go faster requires a lot of different innovations to come together; as per Amdahl’s law,4 there’s no quick fix.

This page is about the cost of measuring that progress:

Suppose AI found, for every deadly disease in the world, a therapy that cuts the chance of its worst outcomes in half compared with the best treatment available today. What would it cost to prove that in pivotal trials?

What is a benevolent coordinator? An idealised planner who runs the world’s pivotal trials as a single programme to best address the global disease burden. So no duplicate or competing trials.

This is only the cost of proving that it all works. Discovery, earlier-phase trials, manufacturing, delivery and access all cost more, and are much harder to predict. Conditions that cause illness but rarely kill, such as depression or back pain, are not on the list, so “every disease” would cost more.

List the diseases, price one pivotal trial for each, then add them up:

From the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study’s list of causes of death from disease, excluding injuries and catch-all groups like “other cardiovascular diseases”, which bundle many conditions no one trial could cover.5 Use one pivotal trial per disease.

Find an RCT that tested what international guidelines recommend today. Among the patients who received it, take their risk of a bad outcome over that trial’s duration, p0.

Work out how many participants a new trial would need to reliably show the risk halving, from p0 to p0/2. Standard hypothesis-testing maths gives the total, N (90% power, 5% significance).

N × $53,904 per participant, summed over diseases. That is Moore et al.’s median cost per participant of a pivotal trial, adjusted to 2026 dollars.6,7 See the maths ↓

Each dot is one way a trial could measure success: a bad event, such as death or a heart attack, that the new treatment would need to make half as common. Rarer events need bigger, more expensive trials. The black tick marks the median cost for each disease, which is what the total adds up. Hover overTap a dot to see the trial its numbers come from.

The headline number surprised me in how small it was. In 2024 the global pharmaceutical industry spent something like on phase 3 trials (in 2026 dollars). I expected the bill for every major disease to be far bigger, even with a benevolent coordinator in charge.

Part of the cost gap is the size of the assumed improvements. Halving the risk of a disease’s worst outcomes is a lot of progress, which needs fewer participants to produce significant results than standard clinical trials. In the pivotal trials establishing today’s best care, the risk of the bad outcomes was cut by a median of . Proving improvements of that size, rather than halvings, would cost about in total.

The other part is redundancy. Many companies compete to treat the same patients: by 2022 there were 5,683 trials testing drugs that block a single immune pathway, PD-1/PD-L1. This got so crowded that combination trials started to outstrip patient demand and the FDA had to call on drugmakers to collaborate to minimise redundancy.8 A newer immune target, TIGIT, has drawn 21 companies developing 30 drugs: about 49,000 patients in 220 trials, at an estimated cost of $3.1–3.6 billion.9 Across the drug R&D pipeline, the number of cancer drugs in development per target rose from 1.8 in 2000 to 9 in 2022.10 The effort is lopsided too in terms of global welfare: cancer accounts for 38% of industry trial starts,11 but 18% of the world’s deaths.5

What would a better-coordinated system look like? During the pandemic, the UK’s RECOVERY trial combined research efforts across NHS hospitals. It showed that dexamethasone reduced deaths among patients hospitalised with COVID-19 without requiring different groups to reproduce trial arms separately.12 I-SPY 2 ran a similar platform trial for breast cancer for more than a decade.13

Other industries have also successfully achieved better coordination to avoid redundancy across firms: in 1987, 14 US chipmakers formed SEMATECH to share pre-competitive manufacturing research. I’m not familiar with the field, but it seems to be widely credited with helping the US recover against Japanese competition.14 Maybe a better system for medicine would look similar: shared trial platforms that companies compete to put their drugs into, rather than dozens of near-identical trials competing for the same patients.

Let p0 be the chance that the bad outcome happens within a fixed follow-up window on today's best care. A therapy that halves it brings the chance down to p1 = p0/2. The trial splits people equally between the new therapy and best care. It must be large enough that a real halving is detected 90% of the time (power), with no more than a 5% chance of a false alarm (two-sided significance). The standard formula for comparing two proportions gives the number of people n in each arm:

Here z1−α/2 = 1.96 and z1−β = 1.28 are the standard normal values for 5% two-sided significance and 90% power, and p̄ = (p0 + p1)/2. The total across both arms is N = 2n. The trial's cost is then N × $53,904: Moore et al.’s median estimated cost per participant across 225 pivotal trials ($41,413), which I assume is in 2019 dollars and adjust by US consumer prices to 2026.6,7 This is a fixed-time approximation, not the event-driven survival design many real trials use.

The gap a trial has to detect, p0 − p1 = p0/2, is squared in the denominator. So the rarer an outcome already is on good care, the more people it takes to see it halve.

PhRMA’s member companies spent 27–39% of their R&D on phase 3 trials in 2024.15 Applying that share to the $288 billion global total16 and adjusting to 2026 dollars7 gives about .

headline: Is Ssense Pivoting to AI Slop?
content:
The green puffer coat isn’t supposed to have a five-inch hook on the left lapel and a weirdly bulging bottom zipper, but that’s how it appeared on the Canadian retailer Ssense.

In a series of Instagram Stories shared on Tuesday by Reese Cooper, the independent designer behind the coat, he claimed Ssense used AI-altered product imagery to misrepresent his designs. In addition to the puffer coat, a gray quarter-zip is missing a front zipper. On a brown shacket, the tape-slotted buttons that Cooper’s team “spent a lot of time developing” disappear in images where the shirt is shown closed. “If you’re gonna Al the whole thing, maybe employ 1 person to keep the slop consistent between the shots?” Cooper wrote. “Seeing the things you’ve made photographed by Ssense used to be such an incredible feeling. This is just insanely disappointing.” Ssense has since removed all items that Cooper alleged were altered from its site.

Cooper isn’t the only designer affected by the stockist using dumb “intelligent” software for its imagery. A printed pair of leather pants by Gerrit Jacob appears on the site with warped graphics and errant seams. On Instagram, Jacob also flagged that the pants’ hem morph into the soles of the model’s shoes, an impossible feat of physics only a not-human would think is passable, and that the G was missing in his brand logo. “Who is errit?” he wrote in a close-up image of his pants.

Responding to Cooper’s and Jacob’s claims, a Ssense spokesperson told The Cut, “Accurate representation of our brand partners and their products is fundamental to Ssense. We recognize that some recent e-commerce imagery did not meet that standard, resulting in inaccuracies in product details. We take full accountability and have taken steps to resolve this issue with urgency.”

Back in July, the Montreal Gazette reported that Ssense laid off its photography, retouching, and hair-and-makeup teams and replaced them with AI, according to an anonymous former employee. The source claimed the retailer is having stylists, the last standing members of its visuals team, take photos of models and then superimposing product images onto their bodies with AI. The former employee also claimed Ssense is “paying for the model’s image rights” in the aim of making digital twins the retailer would own.

The AI blowback comes after a no good, very bad year of press for the retailer. In 2025, after being hit hard by President Trump’s tariffs, Ssense filed for the Canadian equivalent of a Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S., with $371 million CAD in debt. Then came reports it owed its vendors multimillions of dollars, including €3,265,436.96 to luxury brand Jacquemus and $574,058.70 to independent New York label Who Decides War. It’s unclear if the retailer has since paid its creditors.

Integrating AI into its e-commerce photography production now opens up an entirely new can of worms about false advertising. How can a consumer trust the sweater they ordered won’t arrive with a rogue pocket? Discerning whether the crescent moon on a Marine Serre tee is supposed to be split or if it’s an AI agent’s piss-poor job at retouching is too much to ask of a shopper. They’re better off going about things the old-fashioned way — visiting a store in person. That, at least, is an aspect to shopping that AI can never do.

headline: Cops Are Pushing Extremely Corny ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Slop
content:
Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Department, which makes no secret of the kind of maladjusted psychos it's looking for.

“Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” one spot begins. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department, VCPD. You’ll have fun learning the ins and outs of applying excessive force.” The commercial goes on to suggest that cadets will be trained in racial profiling and planting evidence.

Given that blistering analysis of American law enforcement, you might imagine that actual cops aren’t big fans of the latest GTA title, which was released after a 13-year wait on Thursday. Yet as millions of gamers have started to explore every stash house and back alley in the sun-drenched wilderness of a fictionalized South Florida, even police departments have attempted to exploit this monocultural mania to elevate their public messaging or recruit new officers.

It’s a curious strategy given that the series rewards theft and drug dealing while enticing you to run over pedestrians, but evidently the mere presence of law enforcement in the games (as the primary antagonists, mind you) was enough to inspire waves of AI slop celebrating the thin blue line.

An Instagram channel of the San Diego Police Department, for example, on Thursday posted an AI-generated image of an SDPD cruiser set against a sunset over the San Diego Bay. Its neon pinks and purples match the saturated aesthetic of GTA, and in case there was any doubt what the department was going for, the nonsensical phrase “Join San Diego PD VI” appears at the top. “Want to drive a police car, we can make that happen!” reads the caption. “Apply Now!”

Another police department in Washington state shared GTA-like imagery on its Instagram page, encouraging viewers to try “the real-life version” of GTA VI by pursuing a career in law enforcement. “No cheat codes,” the caption advertised. “No respawns. Just real people, real challenges, and a career that makes a difference.” A wave of self-serious GTA slop also flooded the feeds of police departments in Canada, from Edmonton to Toronto—though the Calgary Police Service tried something more lighthearted by having one of their traffic officers react to clips of dangerous and illegal driving maneuvers in the game.

Among police departments that were not seeking to add to their ranks through GTA VI fever, many posted content aimed at reminding people that laws exist in real life. “Keep It In The Game VI,” advised a typical post on the Instagram account of the Glendale Police Department in California, complete with a GTA-fied police cruiser and view of the city. “Follow posted speed limits, respect the law, and keep your wanted level at ZERO!” the caption warned. The Denver Police Department, in similarly scolding fashion, informed followers: “Grand theft auto is still illegal.”

The communications teams for these agencies should have perhaps reconsidered trying to farm engagement and clout from the massive success of GTA VI. As many commenters are noting, the game portrays cops as corrupt and quick to violence. Players have discovered that the Vice City squad will brutalize you if you start filming them during a questionable arrest. One clip showed a cop pulling his weapon on a character who had done nothing worse than stand in the street to take a selfie.

A certain dose of this authoritarian cruelty ought to appeal to the right-wing cranks upset that GTA VI is too “woke” when it comes to gender, race, and politics overall. It’s a little different when the most visible villains of the game are choosing to overlook its vicious take on their profession in order to spam epic social media posts.

Fox News, just for comparison, dutifully took the tired law-and-order line on GTA VI, with talking heads aghast at kids’ exposure to virtual gun violence (never mind actual gun deaths in the US) and an atmosphere of moral depravity. Elon Musk famously declared that he couldn’t play GTA games because they compelled you to shoot cops.

Both stances, however insincere, suggest a modicum of regard for law enforcement that the police departments themselves immediately jettisoned in favor of GTA cringe. They of course won’t win any cool points for it, but at least this way they can pretend to connect with the general population.

More baffling still is that the Russian army has generated its own GTA VI recruitment ads to blast out on its Telegram channel, and NATO has trumpeted its defensive security alliance with military-industrial GTA sludge, boasting that “even the best gamers would have a challenge” eluding fighter jets and submarines. Trying to parse Vice President JD Vance’s depiction of a Trumpian “golden age” with GTA graphics is a fool’s errand. In the most dystopian development of all, a US Army battalion in Georgia granted 43 eligible soldiers four days off to play the new GTA in return for reenlisting for another two years of service.

What do any of these institutions or their missions have to do with a video game where you rob convenience stores in flip-flops? Doesn’t matter. When the zeitgeist is this all-consuming, you fire up ChatGPT and find an angle, no matter how confusing. Surely someone, somewhere, will be tricked into thinking you have anything to do with it.

headline: Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button
content:
Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

The other big change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”

It’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

This change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

headline: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
content:
Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”

It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

headline: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
content:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

Moore said that the most effective means for preventing leakage is to host models using on-premises servers. That option is expensive, though. For those who can’t afford a self-hosted system, the next best option, Moore said, is to receive service directly from a first-tier provider that provides “one contract and a privacy policy to read.” Moore said that even then, there’s no guarantee no data will leak, but that the measure minimizes the chances. AI users should also avoid accepting default provider or reseller pools and instead pick upstream providers themselves.

The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

headline: Daniel Ek backs AI researcher’s fusion power startup. Here’s what they’re building.
content:
Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”
